overview: This file concerns criticism of Japan’s Railway Department following a series of railway accidents in early 1931. A cross-reference sheet directs researchers to Despatch No. 131 in another decimal-file location, while the accompanying excerpt discusses a serious accident on the San’yō Main Line, attributed to excessive speed on a narrow-gauge curve, and Railway Minister Tasuku Egi’s defense of the department before the Diet. Egi argued that accidents had declined substantially since 1924, while acknowledging that the economic depression had reduced railway revenue and constrained improvement spending.

people.name: Eugene H. Dooman
people.role: U.S. diplomatic official in Japan; identified as the sender of Despatch No. 131

subfiles.title: Despatch excerpt on railway accidents and departmental finances
subfiles.about: The excerpt reports criticism of the Railway Department after a fatal San’yō Main Line accident and records Minister Egi’s defense of its safety record and expenditure priorities.
subfiles.summary: After an unrelated opening sentence fragment, the excerpt describes a San’yō Main Line crash that killed nine people and injured fourteen, reportedly because an engineer took a narrow-gauge curve too quickly. Answering a Seiyūkai member in the Diet, Railway Minister Tasuku Egi asserted that accidents had steadily declined and that the previous year’s total was only one-third of the 1924 figure. He acknowledged that the business depression had sharply reduced railway revenue and explained that improvement funds had been concentrated on increasing passenger and freight capacity. A footnote cites Despatch No. 135 of February 9, 1931.

interest: The file offers a compact view of how railway safety, public accountability, and Depression-era fiscal pressures intersected in early-1930s Japan. Particularly useful are the casualty figures, the reported attribution of the crash to excessive speed, and Egi’s statistical defense of the national railway system. The cross-reference and footnote also reveal how related diplomatic reporting was dispersed across the State Department’s decimal filing system, pointing historians toward Despatches Nos. 131 and 135 for fuller context.
